1.sense: A single letter, then an oath sworn on the pen and on what is written with it. The surah takes its name from that pen, and the oath is laid down before the thing it answers, which comes in the next verse. Yasturun is left without a named subject, so the ones doing the writing are not identified.

notes.t: Satara is to draw a line. The plural astur is the ruled lines of a page and the set rows of a plantation, and the same root gives asatir, the word the deniers throw at the revelation in verse 15. The surah swears by writing and is answered with a sneer about writings.
The pen appears in the first revelation as the instrument Allah taught by, which puts this oath on ground already laid.

Early exegetes differ over the letter. Some reports read nun as the inkwell, some as the great fish, and others hold that the disconnected letters are left as letters with no meaning assigned to them. The reports are graded differently and none settles it.
notes.src: the tafsir reports on the disconnected letters; the gradings differ and none settles it

notes.t: A report from Ubada ibn as-Samit has the Prophet ﷺ say that the first thing Allah created was the pen, and that He told it to write. It is carried in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, and both its grading and how it sits beside the reports about the Throne are discussed.
notes.src: Abu Dawud, Book of the Sunna, and Tirmidhi, Book of Qadar, from Ubada ibn as-Samit

links.why: the pen in the first words revealed, as what teaching was given by
trees cut into pens and seven seas of ink, and the words of Allah not running out

2.sense: The answer the oath was sworn for. The charge that the Prophet ﷺ was a man whose mind had been touched, quoted elsewhere in the Qur'an from the mouths of the deniers, is met with a flat denial. The phrase set into the middle of that denial turns the matter over: what has come to him from his Lord is a favour, not an affliction.

notes.t: Majnun is built from jinn, the root of covering and concealment. A janin is the child hidden in the womb, a junna is a shield held in front, and a janna is a garden roofed over by its own foliage. To call a man majnun is to say his reason has been covered.
At-Tur denies the same charge in nearly the same words, adding the soothsayer to it, so the two denials read as one formula.
Al-Hijr quotes the accusation directly, addressed to the one the Reminder was sent down upon.

links.why: the same denial made about him as their companion, someone they had known all his life

3.sense: Against the insult, a wage that does not stop. Mamnun comes from mann, a verb that means both to cut something short and to hold a favour over the head of the one who received it. Both senses are being denied at once: the reward is neither docked nor thrown at him as a debt to be recalled.

notes.t: The exact phrase ajr ghayr mamnun is the standing Qur'anic description of the reward of those who believe and work righteousness. It appears in Fussilat, in At-Tin and in Al-Inshiqaq with the same two words.
Mann in the sense of reproachful giving is what the Qur'an forbids in charity. Reading it here, the reward is given without the giver ever bringing it up again.

links.why: the same unbroken reward, promised there to whoever believes and works righteousness

4.sense: The denial is followed by its opposite stated in the positive. Khuluq is the settled shape a person's conduct has taken, from the root that gives khalq, the making of a thing. What is praised is not one act but the whole formed disposition, and the preposition puts him standing on it as on ground.

notes.t: Khuluq and khalq are one root. Khalq is the outward making of a thing and khuluq is its inward making, so the word treats character as something shaped rather than performed.
Asked about the character of the Prophet ﷺ, Aisha answered that his character was the Qur'an. The report is carried in Muslim and in Ahmad.
notes.src: Muslim, Book of the Prayer of Travellers, from Aisha

notes.t: Al-Imran traces his gentleness with the people to a mercy from Allah, and says that harshness would have scattered them from around him. The character praised here is described there in its effect.

links.why: the same character named as a pattern to be followed

5.sense: The argument is handed over to time. One verb is used twice, once for him and once for them, so the seeing is not his vindication announced to them but a single fact both parties will arrive at. Nothing is asserted here except that the matter will become visible.

notes.t: Absara is to see with the eye and to perceive clearly. The prefix sa- on the first verb sets it in a future that is coming but not dated, which leaves the interval as the test.
Al-Qamar makes the same move against the same charge, telling them they will know tomorrow who the insolent liar is.

links.why: the charge of madness answered there too by a verdict deferred to a day that is coming

6.sense: The sentence begun in the previous verse finishes with its content. What will become visible is which side the derangement was on. The question is put with both parties inside it, which is what makes it an argument rather than a retort.

notes.t: Maftun is a passive participle from fitna, the testing of gold in fire. It carries both the one put to the test and the one whose mind has been turned by it, and the verse holds both.

The grammarians differ over the bi- in bi-ayyikum. Some treat it as adding nothing to the sense, some read al-maftun as a verbal noun so that the question is in which of the two parties the madness lies. The readings change the shape of the sentence, not its outcome.
notes.src: the grammarians on the bi- of bi-ayyikum and on al-maftun read as a verbal noun

7.sense: The verdict is placed where the deniers cannot reach it. Knowledge of who has left the road and who is on it is restricted to Allah by the pronoun huwa standing between the subject and what is said of him. Both halves of the sentence are built the same way, so neither the charge nor the defence is left in human hands.

notes.t: Al-Anam closes a passage with the same words and the same final phrase, bil-muhtadin, so the sentence is a fixed formula in the Qur'an rather than a phrase made for this occasion.
An-Najm carries the first half word for word and ends with biman ihtada instead, after saying that this is the whole reach of their knowledge.
The verse answers verse 6 rather than repeating it. Which of them is afflicted will be seen later; who has strayed is known now, and known by One who is not a party to the quarrel.

links.why: the same sentence used to measure how far the knowledge of the deniers actually goes

8.sense: The first command of the surah, and it follows from the verse before it. Since the judgment belongs to Allah alone, the deniers have nothing to trade with. Tuti is obedience in the sense of going along with, not worship, so what is forbidden is compliance.

notes.t: Al-Insan gives the same instruction joined to the same patience that closes this surah, telling him to be patient for the decision of his Lord and obey neither sinner nor ingrate among them.
Al-Furqan puts the alternative to obeying them as striving against them with the Qur'an itself, a striving described as great.
Two prohibitions run in this passage, one here against the group and one in verse 10 against a type. Between them stands verse 9, which says what the group actually wants.

links.why: the same pair, patience and refusal to comply, in a surah addressed the same way

9.sense: What the deniers were after is stated plainly. The verb is from oil and greasing, and describes smoothing a surface until it gives. Their offer is symmetrical: a little yielding on his side bought with a little yielding on theirs, and the symmetry is the trap.

notes.t: Duhn is oil or fat, and mudahana is the smoothing over of a matter that should have been left rough. The picture is of a hard thing rubbed until it slips.

Al-Isra describes the same pressure without the metaphor. They were close to luring him away from what had been revealed so that he would invent something else, and being made firm is what kept him from inclining a little.

links.why: the whole answer to a proposal of mutual softening, given in one line

10.sense: The second prohibition names a type rather than a man. Nine descriptions run from here to verse 13, and the first pair sets the pattern: a man forever swearing, and a man of no weight. Hallaf is an intensive form, one whose oaths never stop.

notes.t: An oath offered too readily is an admission that the bare word will not be believed. The two descriptions in this verse are cause and effect placed side by side.
Al-Munafiqun describes oaths taken as a shield, sworn to cover something rather than to confirm it.

Mahin is from hawn, lightness and low worth. The same root gives the gentleness praised in the servants of the Merciful, so the word turns on whether the lightness is in the man's step or in his standing.

links.why: the Qur'an on making Allah a target of one's oaths, and what that costs

11.sense: The list moves from what the man swears to what he carries. Hammaz is one who picks at people, by gesture or by word. Mashsha bi-namim is the intensive of walking: not a man who once repeated something, but a man whose occupation is the route between one house and the next.

notes.t: The root of hammaz gives the humaza of Al-Humaza, paired there with lumaza, and the surah opens with woe for exactly this type.
The Prophet ﷺ said that no talebearer will enter the Garden. The report is in Bukhari and Muslim.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Manners, and Muslim, Book of Faith, from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman

notes.t: Namim is named from the faint sound of a whisper. The word for the thing carried is the word for the noise it is carried in.

links.why: the same faultfinding made the subject of a whole short surah

12.sense: The descriptions move outward from speech to conduct. Manna is another intensive, a man whose habit is to block, and khayr covers both wealth and every other good he could let past. Then two flat words, one for crossing the limit and one for the guilt of it.

notes.t: Qaf uses the identical phrase, mannaan lil-khayri mutadin, of the one ordered into the Fire, changing only the last word. The description is a fixed indictment rather than a portrait of one man.
Mana is to prevent and to refuse. Nothing is said about what he does with the good he holds back, only that it stops at him.

links.why: the same three words, spoken as a sentence is passed

13.sense: The last two descriptions, and the phrase between them marks them off as an addition to everything already said. Utull is thick and hard-handed, used of a man who cannot be led. Zanim is the one attached to a people he does not belong to.

notes.t: Zanama are the two loose flaps of skin that hang at a goat's throat or ear. They belong to the animal and do no work, which is the picture behind the word: something joined on and carrying nothing.
The Prophet ﷺ asked whether he should tell them of the people of the Fire, and named every utull, overbearing and arrogant. The report is in Bukhari and Muslim.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Tafsir on this surah, and Muslim, Book of Paradise, from Haritha ibn Wahb

notes.t: Exegetes name a particular man of Quraysh behind the nine descriptions, most often al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and sometimes al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. The reports differ and the verse itself names no one, which leaves the description open to whoever fits it.
notes.src: the tafsir reports naming al-Walid ibn al-Mughira or al-Akhnas ibn Shariq; the verse names no one

14.sense: The reason underneath the nine descriptions. Wealth and sons are what convinced the man he could speak that way. The pair is the Qur'an's standing shorthand for the goods that persuade a person he is past judgment.

notes.t: Al-Muddaththir gives the same account of another such man: extended wealth granted to him, sons present around him, everything smoothed for him, and then obstinacy toward the verses.

Grammarians attach an kana either backward, so that he is not to be obeyed because he has wealth and sons, or forward, so that having wealth and sons is why he calls the verses legends. The reading changes which sentence the reason belongs to.
notes.src: the grammarians on what the clause an kana attaches to

links.why: wealth and children counted up as proof that no punishment is coming

15.sense: What the wealth produces when revelation reaches it. Asatir al-awwalin means old stories written down and passed on, a charge of copying rather than of falsehood outright. The dismissal is the same one the Qur'an quotes from several mouths.

notes.t: Asatir is from s-t-r, the root of the yasturun the surah swore by in verse 1. The writing Allah swears by and the writing they reduce the revelation to are the same word, and the surah has placed them fifteen verses apart.
Al-Mutaffifin carries the sentence word for word, said there of the one who denies the Day of Judgment.

links.why: the same phrase filled out with the accusation that he had them written down and dictated to him

16.sense: The answer to the sneer is a mark. Wasm is the branding of livestock, burnt in where it can be read from a distance and not removed. Khurtum is the trunk or snout of a beast, and using it for a man's nose is the whole insult.

notes.t: Arabic locates pride in the nose. A proud man raises his nose, and a humbled one has it rubbed in the dust, so a mark burnt onto the nose is placed exactly where the arrogance was carried.
Ar-Rahman says the criminals are known by their mark, using the same root as the branding verb here, and taken by the forelocks and the feet.
Exegetes differ over when the brand falls, some placing it in this world and some at the Rising. The verse gives a future tense and no date.
notes.src: the exegetes on whether the branding falls in this world or at the Rising

links.why: criminals identified by a mark on the Day, taken by the forelock

17.sense: The address turns from one man to the deniers as a group, and the argument becomes a story. Their trial is matched to the trial of some owners of a garden who swore an oath over their harvest. Neither the people nor the place is named, and what the verse keeps is the oath and the hour it was sworn for.

notes.t: The root s-r-m runs through the whole passage. They swear to cut the fruit here, the garden becomes like something cut in verse 20, and they call each other harvesters in verse 22. The cutting they intended is the cutting done to them.
Musbihin sets the picking at first light. Going out at that hour is what keeps the poor from being present, which verse 24 states outright.
Al-Kahf tells a parable of two men, one of them the owner of two gardens that are ruined overnight, and puts the same lesson in the mouth of his companion.

links.why: the parable of the man with two gardens, the nearest thing in the Qur'an to this story

18.sense: Two words carry the fault. They swore, and they attached no condition to the oath. Nothing is said about the harvest being theirs to take, only that they spoke about tomorrow as if tomorrow were in their hands.

notes.t: Al-Kahf gives the rule the oath breaks: never say of anything that one will do it tomorrow, except with if Allah wills. The command there follows immediately on a question about a garden and its owners.

Istithna is the grammarians' term for the exception clause in a sentence, which is how most read the verse. Others read it as making no exception for the poor in the crop, taking the fault as withholding rather than presumption. Both readings run into verse 24.
notes.src: the exegetes on the istithna of verse 18, an exception made or an exception withheld

links.why: the due to be given from a harvest on the day it is reaped

19.sense: The answer comes at night and is not described. Ta'if is one who goes around a thing in the dark, a patrol or a caller. The garden is circled the way they had planned to go round it at dawn, and min rabbika swings the sentence back to the Prophet ﷺ in the middle of the story.

notes.t: Tafa is the verb of circling, the same one used for going round a house. What arrives is named only by its motion, so nothing is said about what it was.

Al-Imran likens the spending of the deniers to a wind carrying frost that strikes the tilth of a wrongdoing people and destroys it. The image of a crop taken in a night is already fixed in the Qur'an.

links.why: a reckoning sent from the sky on a garden, leaving bare slippery ground

20.sense: One line for the ruin, and no account of the damage. Asbahat is a verb of morning, so the change is registered at the hour they had chosen for themselves. The comparison is left as a single word.

notes.t: Sarim is read as a field already cut, as the black of night, and as ash. The readings share a picture of everything gone dark and level, and the verb of their oath in verse 17 is from the same root under all of them.
notes.src: the lexicographers on sarim, a field already cut, the black of night, or ash

notes.t: Nothing intervenes between the sleep of verse 19 and the morning of this one. The passage keeps the reader outside the event, exactly where the owners were.

links.why: the garden fallen in on its trellises and the owner turning his hands over

21.sense: The story resumes with them still confident. Tanadaw is calling back and forth across a distance, one household to another at dawn. Musbihin repeats from verse 17, so the hour they swore by has arrived and they do not yet know what it holds.

notes.t: The verse spends its two words on their voices. Between this verse and verse 26 they speak four times, and every word is spoken about a garden that is already gone.

22.sense: Their call is quoted. Ghudu is to set out in the early part of the day, before the sun is high. The condition they attach, if you are harvesters, is the only conditional clause they use, and it is a boast rather than a doubt.

notes.t: Harth is tilled and sown land rather than an orchard, and the same word appears in the parable of the frost in Al-Imran. The word covers what is worked for, which is what the oath was about.
Al-Waqia puts the question to the same kind of confidence: have you seen what you till, do you sow it or do We, and if We willed We would make it broken chaff.

links.why: the tilling of a field taken back to the One who makes it grow

23.sense: The walk to the garden, and the whispering that fills it. Takhafut is the lowering of voices to almost nothing. Since nobody was awake to overhear them, the quiet is between themselves, the manner of people arranging something they would rather not say aloud.

notes.t: Ta-Ha uses the same verb of the raised dead whispering among themselves about how long they stayed in the earth. The word carries voices pitched too low to be sure of.
The plan is not stated here. The verse gives the whispering first and its content in verse 24, so the reader hears the manner before the matter.

24.sense: The whisper is quoted, and it turns out to be a bylaw. No poor man is to get in among them today. Alaykum, upon you, treats a poor man arriving at a harvest as an intrusion rather than a claim.

notes.t: Al-Maun ties the denial of the Day of Judgment directly to shoving the orphan aside and not urging that the poor be fed. The link between disbelief and the closed hand is made there in three verses.
Al-yawma, today, limits the exclusion to one morning. Nothing suggests they had always been like this, only that this once they meant to get the crop in clean.

links.why: not urging the feeding of the poor, given as the reason a man is bound in chains

25.sense: They leave as planned, carrying a purpose and a confidence. Qadirin is the participle of power, and their power extends over a garden that no longer exists. The whole verse is written from inside their expectation.

notes.t: Hard is read as withholding, as a fixed purpose, and as anger. The readings agree that they set out with something settled in them and differ on what it was.
notes.src: the exegetes on hard, read as withholding, as fixed purpose, and as anger

notes.t: Ghadaw here answers the ighdu they called to one another in verse 22. The command and its obedience are one root apart, and both are wasted.

links.why: what the owner of the garden should have said on entering it, and did not

26.sense: The first thing they say on seeing the field is that they have come to the wrong place. Dallun is losing the road, the same verb used in verse 7 for straying from the path. Their first explanation preserves the garden by putting the error in themselves as travellers.

notes.t: The word is exactly the one used of those who stray from the way of Allah in verse 7. On their lips it means only that they have taken a wrong turning, and the next verse cancels that reading.

27.sense: Bal cancels the sentence before it. Not lost, stripped. The correction takes one word and is the first true thing said in the story, though it still describes what happened to them rather than what they did.

notes.t: Al-Waqia puts the identical sentence in the mouths of people whose crop has been turned to chaff, immediately after they say they are burdened with debt. The two passages share both the ruin and the words for it.
Mahrum is a passive participle: deprived by someone. The word admits an agent without naming one, which is as far as they have got.

links.why: the same three words spoken over the same kind of loss

28.sense: One of them had said something at the time and now repeats it. Awsat is the middle one, from wasat, which in Arabic carries the best as well as the centre. His reproach is not that they were greedy but that they left out tasbih, the naming of Allah as free of every defect.

notes.t: The same word makes the community of believers an umma wasat in Al-Baqara, a middle and a best at once. Applied to a man, it names the one who took neither extreme.

Some exegetes read lawla tusabbihun as why do you not say if Allah wills, tying the reproach back to the exception missing in verse 18. Others keep it as glorification in the ordinary sense. The two readings meet in the same omission.
notes.src: the exegetes on lawla tusabbihun, the missing exception or glorification in the ordinary sense

notes.t: He had spoken before, and it did not stop them. The verse records that the objection existed and was not enough, which is why he is the most balanced of them and still standing in the ashes.

29.sense: They say it now. Subhana rabbina is the tasbih they were reproached for leaving out, and it arrives after the harvest instead of before it. The second half moves the fault from the loss to themselves, which is the first time they name it as wrong rather than as deprivation.

notes.t: Zulm is putting a thing where it does not belong. They had put a crop where the poor had a share and their own word where a condition belonged.
Yunus calls out from inside the fish with the same two elements, declaring Allah free of every defect and himself among the wrongdoers. The surah returns to that call in verse 48.

links.why: the same admission made in a different darkness, by a prophet the surah names at its end

30.sense: The confession lasts one verse and then they turn on each other. Yatalawamun is a reciprocal form, blame going both ways at once, which is what happens when a fault was shared and each of them can name the others.

notes.t: As-Saffat uses the same opening words, wa-aqbala baduhum ala badin, and follows them with questioning rather than blaming. The construction is the Qur'an's way of turning a group in on itself.
Saba shows the finished version of this scene, the weak and the arrogant trading the charge back and forth in front of their Lord with nothing decided by it.

links.why: the same mutual blame, staged on the Day when it can no longer change anything

31.sense: The blame between them turns into a sentence they all say. Taghin is stronger than the zalimin of verse 29: not a fault in placing something, but going past a limit altogether. The admission has deepened between the two verses.

notes.t: Tagha is used of water rising over its banks. The root pictures a limit that exists and is passed, which is why it is the Qur'an's word for tyranny.
An-Naziat divides the outcome on this word, giving the Fire as the home of the one who overstepped and preferred the life of this world.

32.sense: The story ends looking forward. Asa keeps it as hope rather than expectation, and no answer is recorded. Raghibun is desiring with the face turned toward what is wanted, and the preposition ila fixes the direction of the wanting.

notes.t: Ragiba fi is to want a thing and ragiba an is to want no part of it, so the sense of the verb turns entirely on its preposition. Here the preposition points at Allah.
Ash-Sharh closes on the same verb as a command, and to your Lord direct your longing, which is the state these men arrive at only after the garden is gone.
The passage stops without saying whether they were given anything better. What it records is the change in them, and that is what the deniers of verse 17 are being shown.

links.why: the same turning, given as an instruction rather than reached through loss

33.sense: The story is closed and applied. Kadhalika points back at the burnt field and forward at Mecca, and the second half raises the scale. The last clause makes ignorance the reason they are not moved by it.

notes.t: Az-Zumar ends a verse with these exact words after describing disgrace in the life of this world, so the sentence is a fixed closing formula.
Law kanu yalamun is a conditional with no answer supplied. What they would do if they knew is left for the reader to finish.

links.why: the same sentence closing a different account of a punishment in this world

34.sense: The counterweight. Janna returns as jannat, plural, after the single garden that was burnt. The decisive phrase is inda rabbihim, with their Lord, which places these gardens where nothing can circle them in the night.

notes.t: The garden of verse 17 was theirs to swear over, and this one is held with their Lord. The surah puts the same word on both sides of the comparison and changes only who holds it.
Sad asks whether the mindful will be made like the corrupt, using the same word muttaqin that opens this verse, and answers by refusing the equation.

35.sense: A question with only one answer, put to people who had assumed the opposite. Muslimin and mujrimin are near rhymes, so the two groups sound alike and are being separated by everything except sound.

notes.t: Al-Jathiya asks the same question of those who commit evils, whether they will be made equal in life and death to those who believe, and calls the assumption behind it an evil judgment.
The verb is jaala, to make or to assign. The question is not whether the two groups differ but whether Allah would treat them as the same, which moves it from observation to justice.

links.why: the same equation refused, with the judgment behind it named as bad judgment

36.sense: The question turns from the conclusion to the faculty behind it. Nothing is said about what they decided; the challenge is to the deciding. Six verses follow, each asking for the ground the judgment stands on.

notes.t: The same sentence closes an argument in Yunus about partners who cannot guide, and stands alone as a whole verse in As-Saffat.
Ma lakum is an idiom of astonishment, what is the matter with you. The verse pairs it with a question about method rather than content.

37.sense: The first of the grounds is checked. A book would be a text with authority behind it, and tadrusun is study, going over it until it is held. The question is not whether they have opinions but whether anything was revealed to them.

notes.t: Fatir asks the same thing of those who claim partners, whether a book was given them so that they stand on clear evidence from it.
The surah swore by the pen and by what is inscribed. The deniers are now asked what they have in writing, and the questions in verses 37 to 41 come back empty.

38.sense: The content such a book would have to carry, quoted as if from its page. Takhayyarun is to pick out what one prefers, so the imagined text would guarantee them their preferences. Stating the claim in that form is the refutation of it.

notes.t: Every scripture the Qur'an describes puts obligations on its holders. A book that awarded its readers whatever they chose would be a record of their wishes, which is what the verse says without saying it.

39.sense: The second ground. Failing a book, a sworn undertaking, and the word for oaths is the one used of the swearer in verse 10. Baligha means reaching all the way, so the covenant they would need must run unbroken to the Day of Rising.

notes.t: Maryam puts the same alternatives to a man confident of wealth in the next life: has he looked into the unseen, or taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.
Their oaths were mentioned first as a habit of the man in verse 10. Here the demand is for an oath in the other direction, sworn by Allah and binding upon Him, which nobody claims to hold.

links.why: the same two grounds, the unseen and a covenant, checked and found absent

40.sense: The Prophet ﷺ is told to put the question directly. Zaim is the man who stands surety for a claim and answers for it if it fails. The demand is not for an argument but for a name.

notes.t: Yusuf uses the word in its plain commercial sense, a herald offering a camel-load to whoever produces the missing cup and saying he is guarantor for it. The word belongs to trade before it belongs to argument.
The command salhum turns a rhetorical sequence into an actual question with an addressee. It also makes the silence that follows part of the argument.

41.sense: The last ground, and the address moves from them to about them. Shuraka here are partners who could underwrite the claim. The challenge is to produce them, which is the Qur'an's usual test of a claim about the unseen.

notes.t: Ash-Shura asks whether they have partners who legislated for them a religion Allah did not permit, which is the same question about the same word.
Four grounds have been checked in five verses: a book, a covenant, a guarantor, a backer. The sequence covers every way a claim can be supported and leaves none standing.

links.why: partners charged with having laid down a religion, and what that would require

42.sense: The day the questions are answered. In Arabic, uncovering the shin describes a crisis at its worst, when a man pulls his garment up to run. On that day they are called to prostrate and the power is not there.

notes.t: Kashafa an saq is an old Arabic idiom for a matter at its hardest, taken from tucking up a robe for flight or for work. Read that way, the verse dates the event by its severity.

Bukhari carries a report from Abu Said al-Khudri about the Day of Rising in which a shin is uncovered and every believer prostrates. Whether this verse speaks of that is discussed among the exegetes, and a reading as the idiom of severity is reported from Ibn Abbas. Early authorities are found on both sides.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Tafsir on this surah, from Abu Said al-Khudri; the idiomatic reading reported from Ibn Abbas

notes.t: Al-Mursalat records the refusal that this inability answers: when they are told to bow, they do not bow.

links.why: the bowing refused while it was still possible

43.sense: The scene held a moment longer. Their eyes are down and humiliation is over them like a garment. The last clause supplies the reason: the same call had come while their bodies were whole and nothing prevented them.

notes.t: Al-Maarij uses the first four words exactly, khashiatan absaruhum tarhaquhum dhilla, describing the same faces on the same day.
Salimun is soundness of body. The verse sets the inability of verse 42 against a health that was spent refusing, so the loss of power is presented as the shape their choice finally took.

links.why: the identical description, closing a passage on the day they were promised

44.sense: The matter is taken out of the hands of the Prophet ﷺ. Fa-dharni leaves Allah and the deniers alone together, which is a form of relief for the one addressed rather than a threat against him. Istidraj is being brought down a stair one step at a time, each step comfortable, the direction unnoticed.

notes.t: Al-Araf carries this sentence word for word, sanastadrijuhum min haythu la yalamun, said there of those who deny the verses.

Daraja is a step or a rank. The tenth form used here means to bring someone along by degrees, and the phrase from where they do not know is what distinguishes it from a punishment they could see coming.
Al-Muzzammil uses the same construction, leave Me and the deniers who have ease, and adds give them a little time.

links.why: the same phrase spoken to the Prophet ﷺ in another Meccan surah, with respite attached

45.sense: The respite is stated as deliberate. Imla is to give a length of time the way rope is let out. Matin is solidly built and firmly attached, so the delay is not weakness in the plan but part of its construction.

notes.t: Al-Araf continues with this verse exactly as it stands here, so verses 44 and 45 reproduce 7:182-183 as a pair.
Matn is the firm ground of a road and the strong flesh along the back. The word is used of the text of a report as against its chain, for the same reason: it is the part that holds.

links.why: the same two verses in sequence, in a Meccan surah on those who deny the signs

46.sense: The questioning resumes, now about motive and cost. Maghram is a debt one is liable for, something owed with nothing received. The question tests whether following the message would leave them financially burdened, and the answer is that it costs them nothing.

notes.t: At-Tur carries this verse and the next word for word, in the same order and with the same am construction.
Yusuf joins the two halves of the surah's closing argument in one sentence: no payment is asked for it, and it is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.

links.why: no fee asked, and the reminder described in the words this surah ends on

47.sense: The last question, and it returns to the pen. Having the unseen and writing it out is exactly what the opening oath was sworn by, and it is the one thing they cannot claim. The surah closes its argument on the instrument it opened with.

notes.t: Yaktubun answers the yasturun of verse 1. The surah swore by writing that records what is given, and ends by asking the deniers whether they hold the unseen and are writing it themselves.
At-Tur has this verse identically, immediately after the verse about payment, so the pair travels together in the Qur'an.

48.sense: The instruction the whole surah has been moving toward, and it comes with a warning attached. Yunus is named only by what happened to him. Makzum describes grief held in with no outlet, and the call he made was made from inside that state.

notes.t: Kazm is tying the mouth of a waterskin shut. The kazimin al-ghayz praised in Al-Imran are those who stopper their rage, and the passive participle here puts Yunus in the state rather than the practice.
Al-Anbiya records the call itself, made in layers of darkness, and names him Dhun-Nun. Nun is a word for the great fish, which is the word the surah opens on.
Al-Insan gives the same command in the same words, fa-sbir li-hukmi rabbika, and follows it with the same refusal to obey that this surah gave in verse 8.

links.why: the full account of Yunus, from the ship to the hundred thousand who believed
the call from the darkness, and the words he called with

49.sense: What the favour prevented. Tadarakahu is one thing catching up with another, a mercy arriving in time. The casting out happened either way; the favour changed the condition he landed in, and the difference is one word.

notes.t: As-Saffat reports the landing itself, cast onto the bare shore while he was ill, with a gourd plant grown over him. The Qur'an gives the event there and the alternative to it here.
Ara is open ground with nothing on it to give cover. The word is chosen for a man coming out of an enclosure into total exposure.

links.why: the shore he was actually cast on, and the shade grown over him there

50.sense: The outcome, in two verbs. Ijtaba is to pick a thing out and gather it to oneself, used in the Qur'an of prophets being selected. The account ends with him placed among the righteous rather than restored to a position, which is the answer to the warning in verse 48.

notes.t: Jaba is to collect, and the eighth form adds choosing for oneself. The selection is described as an act of Allah in both verbs of the verse, with nothing attributed to the man.
Al-Anbiya answers his call, saves him from the distress, and generalises it: thus do We save the believers.

links.why: his people believing, and what came of the mission he had left

51.sense: The surah returns to where it started. Yuzliquna is to make someone slip, and here the slipping is done with looks. The verse ends by quoting the same charge that verse 2 denied, so the whole argument is bracketed by one word.

notes.t: Zalaq is ground so smooth the foot finds nothing to hold, the word used in Al-Kahf for what the ruined garden becomes. Its use with eyes as the instrument is what makes the line strange enough to have been read two ways.

Many exegetes read the verse as the evil eye, a hostile look that harms. Others read it as looks of hatred sharp enough to knock a man off his feet, a known Arabic way of speaking. The verse itself gives only the eyes and the near-slip.
notes.src: the exegetes on yuzliqunaka bi-absarihim, the evil eye or looks of hatred

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that the eye is real. The report is in Bukhari and Muslim, and it establishes the thing without settling what this verse is describing.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Medicine, and Muslim, Book of Greetings, from Abu Hurayra

links.why: the same charge, denied at the opening of the surah before it was quoted at the close

52.sense: The last word on what they were hearing. Dhikr is a reminder, something brought back to a mind that already had it. Lil-alamin widens it past the men who mocked it, so the closing line answers the charge of madness by naming the audience of the message as everyone.

notes.t: The identical sentence closes Sad and stands in At-Takwir, which reaches it just after denying the same charge against the Prophet ﷺ.

Adh-dhikr in verse 51 is what they heard, and dhikr here is what it is. The surah answers their verdict on the messenger by defining the message, and the last two verses hold the two words a line apart.

links.why: the sending itself described in the same reach, a mercy to the worlds
